source.title: AdaShift: Decorrelation and Convergence of Adaptive Learning Rate Methods
source.authors: Zhiming Zhou; Qingru Zhang; Guan-Song Lu; Hongwei Wang; Wei-Nan Zhang; Yong Yu

record.tranche_reason: The study compares adaptive optimizers and reports training and held-out performance on natural-data tasks, using its own optimizer rather than the claim versions’ original interventions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports optimizer comparisons on several natural-data tasks. Its theoretical counterexample results concern online optimization regret, not held-out generalization. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The MNIST experiments include direct SGD–Adam comparisons of held-out accuracy. Most other experiments compare adaptive optimizers with one another and do not test V4's adaptive-versus-SGD claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that temporal decorrelation addresses Adam's non-convergence problem under their assumptions and that AdaShift achieves competitive or sometimes better training and testing performance than Adam.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates a proposed adaptive optimizer that decorrelates gradient statistics by temporal shifting, alongside Adam, AMSGrad, and SGD; it is not a direct reproduction of the optimizer comparisons in V4.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report optimizer-dependent generalization on MNIST and CIFAR-10, and describe AdaShift’s test accuracy as higher than Adam on Tiny-ImageNet and NMT.

fits_no_version.finding: AdaShift variants differ in MNIST MLP generalization; AdaShift matches or exceeds Adam on the reported image and translation tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Choice among adaptive optimizers can affect held-out performance, with AdaShift competitive with or better than Adam in these experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: AdaShift achieves lower DenseNet training loss than Adam.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adaptive optimizer choice affects training optimization performance.

record.problems: The optimizer comparisons report qualitative conclusions from plots, without numerical test-performance values or stated uncertainty. The reported optimizer grid search selects each algorithm’s best result, so tuning scope is not specified as held constant.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible held-out optimizer comparison results were omitted. The online counterexample experiment measures parameter-update direction and convergence, not held-out generalization; training-loss-only comparisons were not included as generalization rows.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization and natural-versus-random held-out accuracy.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of locality.

Adaptive-versus-SGD comparisons on convolutional image classifiers and language tasks; controlled limited-versus-broader tuning; decoupled weight decay; switching optimizers; word-level language modeling. The reported grid-search scope is unspecified.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Dropout, training-set size, and dropout/weight-decay removal with augmentation.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relationship to generalization gaps.
Removing memorized examples versus random examples.

missing.what: A separate held-out comparison of SGD against Adam and AMSGrad for the MNIST MLP. Figure 3 includes these methods, but R2 records only the AdaShift-variant result. Curve rankings cannot be recovered reliably from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. The absent effect in R1 qualifies V4's scope rather than refuting its frequency claim. Online regret, gradient correlations, and ill-conditioned quadratic optimization do not measure any listed generalization effect. The supplied text exposes plot labels and axes but not readable curve values.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and held-out performance under random versus natural labels.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architecture comparisons.
The study does not test language-model optimizer comparisons, broad optimizer tuning, decoupled weight decay, or switching from Adam to SGD.
Sharpness or other measured properties tracking the train-test gap.

rows.subject: Logistic Regression on MNIST
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, max-AdaShift, and non-AdaShift.
rows.baseline: SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, max-AdaShift, and non-AdaShift
rows.value: These learning algorithms achieve very similar final results in terms of both training speed and generalization.
rows.note: The paper describes final generalization as similar across the compared algorithms.
rows.check: The authors explicitly report similar final generalization, including SGD and Adam. Table 5 specifies Adam with beta1=0 and beta2=0.999. Parameter grid search is reported, but its search space and budget are unspecified.

rows.subject: Multilayer Perceptron on MNIST
rows.size_stated: two hidden layers, each with 256 hidden units
rows.operation_detail: Compared SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, max-AdaShift, and non-AdaShift.
rows.note: The text does not state how Adam or SGD compare on test accuracy in this task.
rows.check: The extracted value compares AdaShift variants, not adaptive methods against SGD. Figure 3 includes SGD, but the supplied text does not recover its held-out ranking against Adam. The baseline max-AdaShift is an inferred comparison rather than an explicitly isolated one.

rows.subject: ResNet
rows.value: AdaShift is generally slightly better, especially the test accuracy of ResNet.
rows.note: The explicit comparison is AdaShift versus Adam; the text does not state an SGD comparison here.
rows.check: AdaShift versus Adam measures the proposed method's performance; no SGD comparator is included. Slightly better AdaShift accuracy is not a partial observation of V4.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.value: Adam and AdaShift share competitive results.
rows.note: The text describes the two methods as competitive without specifying a test-accuracy difference.
rows.check: The comparison is between adaptive methods without SGD. Competitive Adam–AdaShift performance cannot establish V4's effect.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.value: AdaShift is generally slightly better, especially ... the training loss of DenseNet.
rows.note: Training loss is not the held-out performance measured by V4.
rows.check: Training loss alone cannot establish held-out generalization, and the comparison lacks SGD. This should not be a standalone claim-result row.

rows.subject: DenseNet
rows.value: AdaShift achieves higher test accuracy than Adam.
rows.note: The comparison reports AdaShift versus Adam, not Adam versus SGD.
rows.check: Higher AdaShift accuracy than Adam evaluates the proposed adaptive optimizer without an SGD comparator.

rows.subject: Neural Machine Translation (NMT)
rows.value: AdaShift achieves a higher BLEU than Adam and AMSGrad.
rows.note: This task extends beyond the image-classification benchmarks in V4; the text does not compare Adam with SGD.
rows.check: The NMT result compares adaptive optimizers only. Language tasks are within V4's broad subject matter, but this comparison does not test its adaptive-versus-SGD claim.

relationships.condition: MNIST logistic regression with the reported grid-selected settings, including Adam with beta1=0
relationships.reason: R1 reports similar final generalization for SGD and adaptive methods, identifying a setting without an adaptive-method penalty; the tuning search space is unspecified.
relationships.display_finding: Reported similar final generalization remains unverified, with the tuning search space unspecified.
